It depends on the specific way in which it's beyond my skill level.

First and most broadly, if it's sincerely that my skill level has not reached a reachable point, then yes - for at least as long as I'm willing to keep putting out the effort, I enjoy it. If, on the other hand, it's that the game is so ridiculously difficult that it's essentially beyond the reach of any normal human, then I'm probably not going to bother for long.

Beyond that, it comes down to specific skills. I have almost no patience for games that are beyond my twitch skills, just because twitch gaming doesn't appeal to me much to begin with. It depends on the game and the genre a bit though. I'm more likely to keep plugging away at a platformer that's beyond my skills, while I don't think I've ever invested more than about 15 minutes into any notably difficult shmup. I generally nope out of them at the first hint of difficulty beyond my (meager) skills. Games that are beyond my strategy skills can go either way. They're the ones I'm probably most likely to keep playing, but they have to engage me, since I'm going to have to invest a fair bit of time and effort into learning all the ins and outs of the game in order to work out the right strategies, but if the game interests me enough, I will do that, no matter how difficult it is.

The Trouble with Transporters - CGP Grey

Why do you need a break in consciousness? Can't "you" just die picoseconds apart and the universe just stores "your" memories chemically in "your" brain so you couldn't notice the difference? Is short-term memory mine, and long-term the string of me(s)? Short-Term is in the brain too, so I wouldn't think so.

Maybe just breaks-in-concentration then? Don't think of Hitler taking a toilet break.

My bed doesn't physically disassemble me at the atomic level though. So even with a consciousness break, I still end up somewhere with all my old memories intact and the ability for self-affirmation. Whether or not that happens with the transporter is a completely different situation. It's been shown that it can copy people, and a consciousness can't be in two places at once.

In terms from the video, when you fall asleep (lose consciousness) that unmeasurable part of you that is your consciousness goes away. When you wake up, it comes back. Where does it go? Does it cease to exist? (Which is a pretty neat trick for something that can't be measured...) When it comes back, is it the same consciousness?

This is far less troubling if you are a poor sleeper, since the days tend to carry into each other.

In reality it doesn't go away, your brain doesn't simply shut off when you go to sleep or are rendered comatose, your consciousness just gets suspended for a lack of a better term (though I know people hate the comparison of the human brain to computers).

The intentionalist response (which is incompatible with dualist ideas about consciousness) is that when you go to sleep, the world continues to exist, and since the mind is all about how you experience that world, the change is simply a matter of degree.

The computer analogy is bad because it locks in the dualism of mind inside the body.

Well I disagree with the notion of it reinforcing duality, though it might be more apt to make the comparison to purpose built computers from the 40s and 50s where the hardware was performing very specific actions.

If you want to avoid mind/body dualism you really ought to avoid using mind-as-a-computer analogies. In a computer, if you are suspending a process you can still find that process somewhere in the physical elements of the machine, and we in fact know that the process exists. If consciousness is like a process that can be suspended, then we should be able to point to it in more than vague terms, but this is where the metaphor breaks down, there is no biological power switch, no biological RAM, sure you can make an analogy of memory to RAM but you can't map numeric memory addresses to anything because biological structures are naturally different.

CGP Grey has, not surprisingly, followed the dualist, or cognitivist, model of mental philosophy - the mind, or consciousness, is separate from our bodies but can experience the phenomena of the world. The problems created by this model are intractable, especially since questions you might ask about how can you show that such-and-such happens to consciousness are always answered with a shrug and the reply: "It can't be measured."

Dualism is a big flop. Intentionalism is where it is at.

New favorite concept (paraphrase):

You can really ever know if you yourself are a conscious, it just seems polite to give everyone else the benefit of the doubt.

This (only having awareness of your own consciousness) is really only a problem if your idea of consciousness is derived from the idea of a Cartesian mind, which is clearly the case for CGP Grey. This consciousness is some kind of internal consciousness that is only accessible to you, maybe it is in your brain or maybe it is non-physical, but even if you were to hook someone else up to a machine that can read their brain and make a representation of their consciousness accessible to you, you aren't accessing their real consciousness, only its representation on a computer screen / simulation / holodeck.

These are problems caused by placing the mind inside the self.
